Hardin is predominantly non-Crow. Under Scenario 1, Hardin is expected to absorb essentially only non-Crow in-migration and will experience the greatest population change of any of the affected communities. This is shown in Figure III-7. A comparison of the figures make it very clear that the future population of Hardin is not so much dependent on whether Westmoreland expands its operation, as on the probabilities of other significant coal development. If Westmoreland's most probable expansion schedule (Scenario 1) coincides with substantial production of other Crow coal, labor demands will cause substantial non-Crow in-migration into Hardin, which will sustain a high level of population growth through 1985. 1/
By 1986, however, permanent production employment associated with coal development on the Westmoreland Resources lease tracts will not be sufficient to maintain the larger population. Substantial out-migration is projected for a period of several years. Unfortunately this implies either that some facility needs must go unmet during the early 1980's or that there will be excess capacity in Hardin's public facilities from 1985 until the mid 1990's, when the slower regional growth rate returns population levels to the previous peak.
A very conspicuous result of the analysis is that none of these problems arise when coal production is limited to Westmoreland's more probable production level of operations (Scenario 1). Such a course would tend to produce a steady growth curve as shown in the left graph in Figure III-7.
